items.prompt: What is the one source of energy that nearly all food chains on Earth ultimately depend on?

options.label: Sunlight
options.feedback: Correct. Sunlight is the original energy source captured by green plants and passed along through food chains.

options.label: The heat of the Earth's core
options.feedback: That heat powers vents in the deep sea, but it supports only tiny, isolated ecosystems, not nearly all life.

options.label: The chemical energy in rocks
options.feedback: Rocks hold minerals, not usable food energy for most living things. Sunlight is the main fuel.

options.label: The movement of wind and water
options.feedback: Wind and water move things but do not feed organisms. Only light, or chemicals in rare vents, provides food energy.

items.ok_line: Nearly every food chain starts with sunlight.
items.ko_line: Vent life is the exception, not the rule.
items.exp_text: Sunlight is captured by green plants and algae to make sugar, and every animal that eats a plant, or eats an animal that ate a plant, is really using that original sunlight. Only a few vent communities use chemical energy from the Earth instead.

items.prompt: Why do many trees lose their leaves in autumn?

options.label: Because the wind blows them off
options.feedback: Wind can knock leaves down, but the tree deliberately cuts them off. The loss is a planned response to shorter days and colder weather.

options.label: Because the leaves die of old age
options.feedback: Leaves do age, but the tree chooses to shed them before winter to save water and energy. Old age alone would not explain the seasonal pattern.

options.label: To save water and energy during winter
options.feedback: Correct. Without leaves, the tree loses less water and does not have to feed many living leaves when sunlight is scarce.

options.label: To give the soil more nutrients
options.feedback: Fallen leaves do return nutrients to the soil, but that is a side effect, not the reason the tree drops them.

items.ok_line: Dropping leaves cuts water loss and energy use.
items.ko_line: The tree cuts its leaves off on purpose.
items.exp_text: In winter, cold and short days mean a leaf cannot make much sugar, but it still loses water through its pores. By dropping every leaf, the tree avoids that water loss and survives the season on stored food.

items.prompt: What is the dark green pigment inside a leaf that captures light energy?

options.label: Carotene
options.feedback: Carotene is an orange pigment that also captures light, but it is not the main green one. The pigment that gives leaves their green colour is chlorophyll.

options.label: Chlorophyll
options.feedback: Correct. Chlorophyll sits inside the leaf's cells and absorbs sunlight to drive the making of sugar.

options.label: Melanin
options.feedback: Melanin is the pigment that gives colour to skin and hair in animals. It does not capture light for plants.

options.label: Xanthophyll
options.feedback: Xanthophyll is a yellow pigment found in leaves, but it is not the main light-catcher. Chlorophyll is the one that makes leaves green.

items.ko_line: Carotene and xanthophyll are extra, not the main one.
items.exp_text: Chlorophyll is packed inside leaf cells and absorbs most colours of light, reflecting green. That captured energy is used to combine water and carbon dioxide into sugar, which is why chlorophyll is essential to plant life.

items.prompt: In which part of a green plant does the food-making process mainly take place?

options.label: The roots
options.feedback: Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil, but they do not make food. Leaves are the main food-making organs.

options.label: The stem
options.feedback: Stems carry water and sugar between roots and leaves, but they are not the main food factories. That job belongs to leaves.

options.label: The flowers
options.feedback: Flowers are for reproduction, not for making food. Green leaves are where sunlight is captured.

options.label: The leaves
options.feedback: Correct. Leaves are flat and thin, full of chlorophyll, and arranged to catch as much light as possible, so they are the main sugar producers.

items.ok_line: Leaves capture light and make sugar.
items.ko_line: They carry materials, not make food.
items.exp_text: Green leaves contain chlorophyll and are shaped to absorb maximum sunlight. They take in carbon dioxide through their pores and water from the roots, then use light to build sugar. That is why leaves are the food-making parts of a plant.

items.prompt: What happens to a plant that is kept in complete darkness for many days?

options.label: It uses up stored food and eventually weakens
options.feedback: Correct. Without light it cannot make new sugar, so it must live on what it stored, and it grows pale and thin as those stores run out.

options.label: It stays healthy because it can rest
options.feedback: Plants do not eat or rest like animals. They need light to make food, so darkness starves them.

options.label: It turns yellow because it makes too much chlorophyll
options.feedback: Chlorophyll needs light to be made and maintained. In darkness, plants lose their green colour, not gain more of it.

options.label: It grows faster because there is no heat from the sun
options.feedback: Darkness does not speed up growth. Without light, growth stops and the plant weakens.

items.ok_line: A dark plant lives on stored food and fades.
items.ko_line: The plant must spend its savings and weaken.
items.exp_title: What darkness does to a plant
items.exp_text: A plant in the dark cannot photosynthesise, so it burns through the sugar stored in its roots and stem. Unable to make more, it grows pale, spindly, and eventually dies if the darkness lasts too long.

items.prompt: What is the main gas that a plant pulls in through its leaves to make food?

options.label: Oxygen
options.feedback: Oxygen is released as a waste product during food-making. The plant takes in carbon dioxide, not oxygen, for the main process.

options.label: Nitrogen
options.feedback: Nitrogen is abundant in the air but plants do not use it from the air for food. They take in carbon dioxide through their leaves.

options.label: Carbon dioxide
options.feedback: Correct. Carbon dioxide enters through the leaf pores and combines with water using light energy to build sugar.

options.label: Hydrogen
options.feedback: Hydrogen is part of water, but it is not a separate gas that a leaf takes in. Carbon dioxide is the gas absorbed from the air.

items.ok_line: Carbon dioxide enters leaves to make sugar.
items.ko_line: Those gases are not used for food-making.
items.exp_text: Leaves have tiny pores on their undersides that let carbon dioxide from the air diffuse inside. There, along with water, it is converted into sugar using sunlight. Oxygen is the by-product that goes out the same way.

items.prompt: Why does a potted plant placed near a window gradually tilt its stem toward the window?

options.label: Because the stem is pulled by the light
options.feedback: Light does not pull stems. The stem grows more on the dark side, which pushes the tip toward the light.

options.label: Because cells on the shady side grow longer
options.feedback: Correct. The dark side of the stem stretches faster, bending the whole stem toward the brighter side.

options.label: Because the leaves push the stem sideways
options.feedback: Leaves do not push stems. The bending happens inside the stem itself due to uneven growth.

options.label: Because the potting soil shifts toward the window
options.feedback: Soil does not move with light. The plant's own growth pattern causes the leaning.

items.ok_line: Shady-side cells stretch, bending the stem.
items.ko_line: It is uneven growth, not attraction.
items.exp_text: A plant hormone moves to the dark side of the stem and makes its cells there elongate. With one side stretched and the other not, the stem curves toward the light source, which is called phototropism.

items.prompt: What is the name for a plant that needs long days and short nights to flower?

options.label: A short-day plant
options.feedback: A short-day plant flowers when nights are long, the opposite. A long-day plant flowers with short nights and long days.

options.label: A day-neutral plant
options.feedback: A day-neutral plant flowers regardless of day length. The one you are describing depends on long days.

options.label: A continuous-light plant
options.feedback: There is no such standard term. The correct term describes the response to day length, not to continuous light.

options.label: A long-day plant
options.feedback: Correct. Long-day plants such as many summer flowers need more daylight than darkness to trigger flowering.

items.ok_line: Long-day plants bloom with short nights.
items.exp_text: A long-day plant measures the dark period and only flowers when nights are short enough, which happens in late spring and summer. The name refers to the long daylight part of the cycle, not to needing endless sun.

items.prompt: What does a plant's internal clock use, rather than temperature, to tell the season?

options.label: The length of day or night
options.feedback: Correct. Day length changes predictably with the seasons, so plants use it as a reliable signal for when to flower or drop leaves.

options.label: The amount of rainfall
options.feedback: Rain is unpredictable and varies from year to year. Plants primarily use day length, a steady signal.

options.label: The direction of the wind
options.feedback: Wind direction has no seasonal pattern that plants can rely on for timing. Day length is the key.

options.label: The colour of the sky
options.feedback: Sky colour changes with weather, not reliably with seasons. Day length is the constant measure.

items.ok_line: Plants read the dark and light hours.
items.ko_line: Those are too changeable for timing.
items.exp_text: Leaves contain pigments that measure how long the night lasts. That measurement tells the plant whether it is spring, summer, or autumn, better than temperature, which can vary wildly from year to year.

items.prompt: Why do many flowers open in the morning and close at night?

options.label: To save water by not losing it during the day
options.feedback: Flowers lose water when open, so closing at night actually saves water. Opening in the morning is for pollinators and light, not to waste water.

options.label: To keep warm during the cold night
options.feedback: Some flowers do close for warmth, but the main reason for opening in the morning is to attract daytime visitors and catch light.

options.label: To match the activity of daytime pollinators
options.feedback: Correct. By opening in daylight, flowers are ready for bees and other insects that fly during the day, and closing at night protects them from night visitors and dew.

options.label: To let the leaves get more sunlight
options.feedback: Flowers are not for catching sunlight; leaves are. Flowers open for pollination.

items.ko_line: It is about matching pollinator schedules.
items.exp_text: Many flowers have a daily rhythm tied to light. They open in the morning when bees, butterflies, and birds are active, and fold shut at night when those visitors are gone, which also protects pollen from moisture.
